title: Atman and Brahman: Teachers in the Forest
bigQuestion: What do the Upanishads teach about the self and ultimate reality, and how have Hindu schools read those teachings differently?

story.title: Salt in the Water
story.kicker: A father asks his son to find salt he cannot see.
paragraphs: Svetaketu has come home after twelve years of study. He is twenty-four and proud of all he knows. His father, Uddalaka, watches him for a while. Then he asks a question: have you learned the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown becomes known?

Svetaketu has not. So his father begins to teach. One evening he hands his son a lump of salt. "Put this in a cup of water," he says, "and come to me in the morning." Svetaketu does as he is told, though he does not yet see the point.

In the morning his father says, "Bring me the salt." Svetaketu looks in the cup. He cannot see any salt. It has dissolved. "Taste the water from the top," his father says. It is salty. "From the middle." Salty. "From the bottom." Salty still.

"In the same way," his father says, "you do not see the true being here, yet it is here." He ends, as he has ended other lessons, with words that have been repeated for many centuries. Many readers render them in English as: "That art thou."

This story comes from the Chandogya Upanishad, chapter 6. Hindu teachers, students and philosophers have discussed it for well over two thousand years. They do not all agree on what it means. You will meet several of their readings in this chapter.
story.think: Why do you think Uddalaka used salt and water instead of just telling his son the answer?

lessons.title: Sitting Near a Teacher
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads are texts of teachings and dialogues, the oldest composed c. 800–200 BCE by scholarly estimate.
reading: Picture a student sitting on the ground at a teacher's feet, asking questions. Many scholars link the word *Upanishad* to this picture: sitting down near. Others explain it as a hidden teaching. Both ideas fit the texts.

The Upanishads are the last layer of the Vedas. Tradition lists more than a hundred, but about a dozen are called the principal Upanishads. They include the Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, Katha, Isha and Mundaka.

Scholars date the oldest ones, the Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya, to about 800–500 BCE. Others came later, some after 200 BCE. Many Hindus regard them, like all the Vedas, as shruti, eternal truth that was heard by seers rather than invented.

The Upanishads are not a single story. They mix dialogues, riddles, lists and short poems. Many follow a teacher and a student, a husband and a wife, or a king and a sage as they ask what is truly real.

words.d: a Vedic text of teachings about the self and ultimate reality; the word may mean 'sitting near'
the dozen or so oldest and most studied Upanishads
a conversation between two or more people, used to teach ideas

lessons.title: Vedanta: The End of the Veda
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads are called Vedanta, the end of the Veda, and they became the basis of the Vedanta schools.
reading: Remember the four layers of each Veda. The Upanishads come last. So they are called *Vedanta*, which means the end of the Veda. Many Hindus also read end as goal: the Upanishads show what the whole Veda aims at.
Later, Hindu thinkers built whole schools on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras. These three are called the three starting points. The schools are also called Vedanta.

The most famous teachers include Shankara (c. 8th century CE), Ramanuja (c. 11th–12th century) and Madhva (c. 13th century). Each read the Upanishads differently. Their followers still debate these readings today.

words.d: 'end of the Veda'; the Upanishads, and the schools of thought built on them

lessons.title: Max Müller's Translations
lessons.mainIdea: F. Max Müller translated twelve principal Upanishads into English in the Sacred Books of the East (1879 and 1884).
reading: In the 1870s, a German-born scholar at Oxford named F. Max Müller began a huge project. He edited a series called the *Sacred Books of the East*. It put texts from many Asian religions into English, fifty volumes in all.

Müller himself translated the Upanishads in volumes 1 (1879) and 15 (1884). These books are now in the public domain, so they can be quoted freely. They helped many Western readers meet the Upanishads for the first time.

Müller's English sounds old today, with thee and thou. Some of his views about India reflected the attitudes of his time. Modern translators such as Patrick Olivelle offer newer versions. Readers often compare them.

words.d: a 50-volume series of English translations of Asian religious texts, edited by Max Müller
a text put into another language

look.title: Two Translations

look.prompt: How do these English versions of the same Sanskrit words differ? Why might the wording change what a reader thinks the passage means?

lessons.title: Atman: The Self
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads use the word atman for the true self, which they describe as deeper than body and mind.
reading: Ask yourself: who am I? My body? My thoughts? My name? The Upanishads ask this again and again. Their answer points to the *atman*, the true self. It is a word you will meet on almost every page.

Many passages say the atman is not the body, which changes and dies, and not even the mind, which changes all day. The Katha Upanishad says the self is not born and does not die. Hindus who follow these texts believe the atman is what passes from life to life in samsara.

The Upanishads say the atman is hard to see, like the salt in water. Knowing it, they teach, brings freedom. This knowing is not just learning facts. The texts describe it as a deep, direct understanding.

words.d: the true self; in the Upanishads, the deepest self beyond body and mind
who a person really is; in the Upanishads, the atman

lessons.title: Brahman: Ultimate Reality
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads use Brahman for the ultimate reality that is the ground of everything.
reading: In the salt story, Uddalaka speaks of a fine essence in everything. The Upanishads name the deepest reality *Brahman*. It is not one god among many. The texts describe it as the source and ground of all that is.

The Upanishads often say Brahman cannot be fully described. One famous phrase in the Brihadaranyaka is neti neti, not this, not this. Whatever you point to, the teacher says, Brahman is more than that.

Other passages describe Brahman positively, as being, awareness and bliss. Later Hindu teachers joined these as sat-chit-ananda. Many Vaishnavas and Shaivas identify Brahman with Vishnu or Shiva as a loving, personal God.

words.d: in the Upanishads, the ultimate reality and ground of everything
'not this, not this'; a way the Upanishads say Brahman is beyond every description
being, awareness and bliss; a later phrase describing Brahman

lessons.title: That Art Thou
lessons.mainIdea: The Chandogya Upanishad's teaching, often rendered 'That art thou' (6.8.7), links the self to ultimate reality.
reading: Nine times in Chandogya Upanishad chapter 6, Uddalaka ends a lesson with the same Sanskrit words: *tat tvam asi*. Many readers render them 'That art thou' or 'You are that.' The first time is in 6.8.7.
What is that? Uddalaka has been speaking of the fine essence in all things, the true being. So many readers take the phrase to say that the self, atman, is linked at its root to Brahman.

Not everyone reads the grammar the same way. Some later readers split the words differently to mean 'you are not that.' This small difference shows how one line can carry very different ideas. You will see the main readings in the next section.

words.d: Sanskrit words from Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, often rendered 'That art thou'
the most basic, inner nature of something

lessons.title: Shankara: Not Two
lessons.mainIdea: Shankara's Advaita Vedanta reads the Upanishads to say the self and Brahman are not two but one.
reading: Shankara, a teacher from Kerala generally dated to the 8th century CE, wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras. His school is *Advaita Vedanta*. Advaita means not two.

Shankara taught that Brahman alone is fully real. He read 'That art thou' to mean the atman is identical to Brahman. The world of many separate things, he said, is appearance, called maya. Knowing the truth ends ignorance and brings moksha.

Advaita has been very influential. Swami Vivekananda, who spoke in Chicago in 1893, taught a form of it. Many Hindus follow other schools, though, and argue that Shankara's reading leaves too little room for a personal God.

words.d: 'not two'; Shankara's school, which teaches that atman and Brahman are one
in Advaita, the appearance of a world of many separate things
a book that explains another text line by line

lessons.title: Ramanuja and Madhva
lessons.mainIdea: Ramanuja and Madhva read the same Upanishads as teaching a loving relationship between the soul and a personal God.
reading: Ramanuja, a Tamil teacher of the 11th–12th century, read the Upanishads differently. His school is *Vishishtadvaita*, qualified non-dualism. He taught that souls and the world are real, like the body of God, who is Vishnu.
For Ramanuja, 'That art thou' means the self belongs to Brahman as a part belongs to a whole, not that they are the same. Moksha is loving service of God, reached through bhakti and God's grace.

Madhva, of the 13th century, went further. His school is *Dvaita*, dualism. He taught that God, souls and the world are forever distinct. Both schools remain alive in South India and beyond. Followers of each read the same verses with care and conviction.

words.d: Ramanuja's 'qualified non-dualism': souls are real parts of God's body
Madhva's 'dualism': God, souls and the world are forever distinct
help or love freely given by God, in devotional teaching

look.title: Three Readings Side by Side

lessons.title: Lead Me from the Unreal
lessons.mainIdea: A short prayer from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (1.3.28) is still recited widely by Hindus today.
reading: Many Hindu schools and gatherings open or close with a short Sanskrit prayer. It begins asato ma sad gamaya. It comes from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28, where it is chanted as part of a ritual.

The prayer asks three things. Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to immortality. The text itself explains that the unreal and darkness mean death, and the real and light mean immortality.

The prayer shows how Upanishad words live on in daily use. Many families teach it to children. It is printed on school walls in India and recited at interfaith events. People of different schools each find their own meaning in it.

words.d: freedom from death; living forever
'lead me from the unreal to the real', the opening of Brihadaranyaka 1.3.28

lessons.title: The Upanishads and the World
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads have shaped Hindu thought and have drawn readers from around the world.
reading: In 1657 a Mughal prince, Dara Shikoh, had fifty Upanishads translated into Persian. He believed they shared truths with his own Sufi Islamic tradition. A French scholar later put that Persian version into Latin.

The German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer read the Latin version in the 1800s and praised it highly. American writers like Ralph Waldo Emerson were also drawn to Upanishad ideas, which they read in translation.

In 1893, Swami Vivekananda brought Vedanta to Chicago. He founded Vedanta Societies in the United States soon after. For many Hindus, though, the Upanishads matter most as living teaching, studied with a teacher and lived with care.
